Laura Luu, Fo Niemi et Kyungseo Min, rép: Laura Luu, Fo Niemi and Kyungseo Min are documenting cases of anti-Asian racism in Quebec.
Une première a eu lieu vendredi dernier: A first took place last Friday in the history of Montréal and its Asian communities.
On a en effet annoncé en conférence de p: At a press conference, it was announced that a motion will be tabled at Montréal city council to unanimously denounce the rise of anti-Asian racism in Montréal in the wake of the COVID-19 pandemic. Several groups joined the Centre de recherche-action sur les relations raciales (CRARR) in supporting the resolution, including the Concordia Student Union (which has 37,100 members), the McGill University student association, the Philippine Association of Montreal and Suburbs, the Chinois progressistes du Québec and the Conseil de développement économique du Quartier chinois de Montréal.
« Devant la recrudescence des actes hain: “Faced with the surge in hateful acts against people of Asian origin or appearance, and the inaction of Montréal authorities and the Service de police de la Ville de Montréal (SPVM), CRARR proposed a draft resolution to me asking the City of Montréal to condemn anti-Asian racism,” explained Marvin Rotrand, independent city councillor for Côte-des-Neiges–Notre-Dame-de-Grâce. “I accepted right away, because history shows that silence is the worst response, and even encourages the spread of racial hatred.”
Cette motion demande que toutes les mesu: The motion calls for all measures to be taken to protect these Montrealers from any form of harassment and violence across the island. A vote on the resolution will be held on June 15.
Fo Niemi, directeur général du CRARR, es: Fo Niemi, executive director of CRARR, is optimistic, though not wearing rose-coloured glasses. “What is happening in the United States, with the police and Black communities, is helping to wake a lot of people up, but we always have to be careful, we have to stay vigilant,” he says. “In debates about racism, or what we call anti-racism, there is still a lot of resistance. Many people refuse to believe that Asians can be victims of racism. If there were an arson attack in Chinatown, or if someone got stabbed there, then some people would wake up, but unfortunately it would be a little late.
On a beaucoup à faire. »Des actes crimin: “We have a lot to do.” There have nevertheless been criminal acts targeting Asian communities in Montréal since February. Notably, a Korean man was stabbed in March on Décarie Boulevard. According to information gathered from the Consulate General of the Republic of Korea in Montréal, he decided to return to Korea with his family. Before the COVID-19 pandemic, CRARR received an average of two or three complaints a month about hateful acts against people of Asian origin. In the last three months, it has received 18. Vancouver police have recorded 29 over the past three months. The SPVM has only vague information on hate crimes.
Du côté fédéral, la question fait aussi: At the federal level, the issue is also gaining ground. Minister of Diversity and Inclusion and Youth Bardish Chagger held a virtual round table a few weeks ago with about a hundred people from Asian communities to discuss the pan-Canadian plan to fight anti-Asian racism. And Prime Minister Trudeau denounced this type of racism in one of his statements. What shocks many Asian Quebecers, then, is rather the way the provincial government is handling the issue of racism, namely by advocating a “quiet evolution.”
Ils voient là un déni du racisme systémi: They see in this a denial of systemic racism that can only damage the government’s credibility when it comes to recognizing racism, especially racism targeting a group considered well integrated. Contacted about this, François Legault’s office said that Mr. Arruda mentioned it at a press briefing early in the pandemic. An official statement on the subject is nevertheless still awaited. Fo Niemi laments the slowness. “In British Columbia, the premier and the chief of police took concrete measures; in Alberta, it was the chair of the Alberta Human Rights Commission who spoke out in favour of anti-racist action, but in Quebec, we have almost nothing. Yes, there is a plan to fight discrimination and racism, the government promises to ‘take action,’ but without recognizing systemic racism.”
Des pagodes vandalisées dans le quartier: Pagodas vandalized in the Rosemont neighbourhood and in Côte-des-Neiges, a door spray-painted with the words “COVID-19 chinese” in Ahuntsic-Cartierville, verbal attacks on Asian women when they go out to run errands – these are a few examples of the xenophobia that has been pervading Quebec for the past few months. “You should think about going back to your country instead of being careless and coming to infect us all,” an Asian woman was told on March 19 in a pharmacy in Alma, in Saguenay–Lac-Saint-Jean, according to a report cataloguing the testimonies of the many victims of anti-Asian racism in the province. The study is being carried out by a Montréal woman of Korean origin, Kyungseo Min, in collaboration with a McGill law student, Lily Wang.
Kyungseo raconte : « Ce que nous avons c: Kyungseo says: “What we found in this study is that it’s mostly Asian women who have been verbally attacked, maybe because we’re an easy target.
Nous sommes plus vulnérables, moins susc: “We’re more vulnerable, less likely to fight back or file a complaint… we tend to walk away, ignore unpleasant situations or flee them. That’s why it’s so easy for aggressors to threaten us,” explains the 26-year-old writer, who was born in South Korea and immigrated to Calgary with her family at the age of 6. Collecting the stories that none of the victims, for one reason or another, reported to the police; bringing together voices that would otherwise have been lost – that is what Kyungseo and her colleague Lily have been doing for months to show that anti-Asian racism is not an isolated incident: it spreads insidiously through society, whether on social media or in the street. It has existed in this country for hundreds of years, but the coronavirus has stoked it. And while a new generation of Asians is now its target, it does not intend to stay silent.
Réaliser un recueil de données sur la ba: Compiling data based on ethnic origin is difficult for Asian communities, especially among older people. Police services do not reach out to community services to offer help and encourage people to take part in preventing hate crimes. There are also the stereotypes aimed at most Asian people, according to which it is almost unthinkable that they could be victims of racism. They are, in fact, considered docile, obedient, hard-working, quiet.
Elles représentent un modèle d’intégrati: They represent a model of integration marked by humility and discretion, two traits that almost all Asian families pass on to their children, which does nothing to encourage speaking out. “Our parents have always told us to keep quiet, to ignore it and to keep moving forward despite the insults. But we’ve reached a point, especially with COVID, where we have no choice but to stop pressing the ‘ignore’ button, and instead learn, with our Quebec values, to speak up, to protect ourselves and to stand up against injustice,” says Laura Luu, administrator of the Facebook page called Groupe d’entraide contre le racisme envers les Asiatiques au Québec. The racism experienced by people born in Quebec with Asian roots, like Laura Luu, is a relatively recent phenomenon for many of these Quebecers, who had never been victims of this scourge before. The Facebook page Groupe d’entraide contre le racisme envers les Asiatiques au Québec has more than 5,000 members and is a place where people can report reprehensible acts, but also find solutions for coping with the fear tied to these verbal, even physical, attacks.
« Moi, ce qui m’inquiétait le plus, c’ét: “What worried me the most was whether my mother, my family or the older generations would talk about it if it happened to them. Because they won’t talk about it, and I wonder what they’ll do with it,” laments Laura, a woman of Vietnamese origin who recently became a mother. May Chiu echoes the concern. A lawyer and anti-racist activist for decades, she is also a member of the Chinois progressistes du Québec. She worries about elderly people of Asian origin who speak neither French nor English. “Are they able to grasp the scale of this crisis?
Mon père ne comprenait pas pourquoi pers: “My father didn’t understand why no one had come to visit him for several weeks,” explains May Chiu, who was only able to start communicating again with her 89-year-old father, who lives at the Centre d’hébergement Jean-De La Lande, a few weeks ago. The facility had not followed up with her.
« Mai a été le Mois du patrimoine asiati: “May was Asian Heritage Month in Canada, and with the COVID crisis, people are looking for their place, as well as ways to mobilize and protest without having to leave the house. Many members of our communities feel that we are on the defensive and that the spread of hatred prevents victims from sharing their stories and feeling a sense of empowerment. There is great diversity within Asian communities. So we need an intersectional approach to tackle the root of the problem,” says May Chiu, who is currently working on a guide to provide resources to Asian people.
